aos.name: Unit 1 AoS 1 · How do the structures of materials explain their properties?

topics.title: Atoms, isotopes and electron configuration
points: Protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1) are in the nucleus; electrons (−1, almost no mass) are in shells.
Atomic number \(Z\) = protons. Mass number \(A\) = protons + neutrons, so neutrons \(= A - Z\).
Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of an element’s isotopes on the carbon-12 = 12 scale.
Shell n holds up to 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18, 32). Subshells: s holds 2, p 6, d 10. Fill order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d.
Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d.
topics.explain: Explain why sodium-23 and sodium-24 are the same element but have different masses.

qs.q: How many neutrons are in an atom of \({}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\) (\(Z = 17\))?
Which is the subshell configuration of a sulfur atom (\(Z = 16\))?
Chlorine is \(75.8\%\) Cl-35 (\(34.97\)) and \(24.2\%\) Cl-37 (\(36.97\)). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
qs.e: Multiply each isotopic mass by its fractional abundance and add.

qs.q: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in \({}^{39}\mathrm{K}^{+}\) (\(Z = 19\))?
qs.e: A \(+1\) ion has lost one electron: \(19 - 1 = 18\) electrons.

qs.q: Why do elements produce line emission spectra?
qs.a: Electrons absorb energy and jump to higher energy levels. When they fall back they emit light with exact energies (the differences between levels), so only certain wavelengths appear.
qs.e: Each element has its own set of energy levels, so its spectrum is a fingerprint (flame tests).

topics.title: Periodic table trends
points: Period = number of occupied shells. Group = same number of valence electrons, so similar chemistry.
\(\text{Core charge} = \text{protons} - \text{inner-shell electrons}\). It increases across a period and stays the same down a group.
Across a period: atomic radius decreases, electronegativity and first ionisation energy increase, metallic character decreases.
Down a group: an extra shell, so radius increases, electronegativity and ionisation energy decrease, metallic character increases.
Metals get more reactive down a group; non-metals get less reactive down a group.
topics.explain: Use core charge to explain why fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen.

qs.q: Which has the largest atomic radius?
qs.e: Radius decreases across period 3 as core charge rises, so Na is largest.

qs.q: What is the core charge of a chlorine atom?
Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
qs.a: Potassium’s valence electron is in a shell further from the nucleus (4th vs 3rd) with the same core charge, so it is held less strongly and lost more easily.

qs.q: Going down group 17, electronegativity…
qs.e: Valence electrons are further from the nucleus, so bonding electrons are attracted less.

topics.title: Covalent bonding, shapes and polarity
points: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms. Double and triple bonds share 2 or 3 pairs.
Lewis structures: count valence electrons, put the least electronegative atom (never H) in the centre, add bonds, then lone pairs.
VSEPR: electron groups repel. 2 groups linear 180°; 3 trigonal planar 120°; 4 tetrahedral 109.5°; 4 with 1 lone pair pyramidal; 4 with 2 lone pairs V-shaped.
A polar bond joins atoms of different electronegativity. A molecule is polar only if its shape is uneven (H₂O, NH₃); symmetrical molecules cancel out (CO₂, CH₄).
Forces between molecules: dispersion (all molecules, grows with size) < dipole–dipole (polar) < hydrogen bonding (H on N, O or F).
Covalent network lattices: diamond (4 bonds each, very hard, no conduction), graphite (3 bonds each, delocalised electrons conduct, layers slide).
topics.explain: Explain why water boils at 100 °C but methane boils at −162 °C.

qs.q: What is the shape of an ammonia (NH₃) molecule?
qs.e: 4 electron groups, 1 lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.

qs.q: Which molecule is non-polar even though it has polar bonds?
qs.e: CO₂ is linear, so the two C=O dipoles cancel.

qs.q: Which intermolecular force exists between all molecules?
qs.e: Temporary dipoles form in every molecule.

qs.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
qs.a: In graphite each carbon bonds to 3 others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move. In diamond all 4 valence electrons are in bonds, so no charged particles can move.

qs.q: When water boils, what is broken: covalent bonds or hydrogen bonds?
qs.a: Hydrogen bonds between molecules. The O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

topics.title: Metals
points: Metallic bonding: a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised valence electrons, held by electrostatic attraction.
Properties: conduct (free electrons), malleable and ductile (layers slide, electrons still hold them), lustrous, high melting points.
Work hardening (cold) gives small crystals: harder, brittle. Annealing (heat, cool slowly): large crystals, softer. Quenching (cool fast): hard, brittle. Tempering reheats gently: tough.
Alloys: substitutional (similar-sized atoms, brass) or interstitial (small atoms such as C in steel). Both stop layers sliding.
Reactive metals: metal + water → hydroxide + H₂. Recycling metals saves energy and supports a circular economy.
topics.explain: Use the metallic bonding model to explain why metals bend instead of shattering.

qs.q: Which treatment makes a metal softer and more malleable?
qs.e: Slow cooling grows large crystals with fewer boundaries.

qs.q: Why does steel (iron with carbon) resist bending more than pure iron?
qs.a: Small carbon atoms sit in gaps between iron cations (interstitial alloy), disrupting the layers so they cannot slide easily.

qs.q: Metals conduct electricity because…
o: their ions move through the lattice
qs.e: Cations stay fixed; the electrons carry charge.

topics.title: Ionic compounds and precipitation
points: Metals lose electrons (cations), non-metals gain them (anions), reaching noble-gas configurations. Ions form a 3D crystal lattice.
Hard, high melting point, brittle (shifted layers put like charges together). Conduct only when molten or dissolved.
Formulas balance charge: Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃. Roman numerals show variable charge: copper(II) sulfate.
Learn: NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, CH₃COO⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻.
SNAPE ions (sodium, nitrate, ammonium, potassium, ethanoate) are always soluble. CHOPS (carbonate, hydroxide, oxide, phosphate, sulfide) are usually insoluble.
Ionic equations leave out spectator ions: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
topics.explain: Explain why solid salt does not conduct but salt water does.

qs.q: What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
Which pair of solutions forms a precipitate when mixed?
Write the ionic equation for BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq).
qs.e: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions.

qs.q: Ionic solids are brittle because…
o: a shift lines up like charges, which repel

qs.q: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide?
qs.e: Fe³⁺ and O²⁻: swap and simplify, 2 : 3.

topics.title: Dissolving and chromatography
points: Like dissolves like. Ionic solids dissolve in water through ion–dipole attractions; small polar molecules form hydrogen bonds with water.
Chromatography separates by competition between adsorbing to the stationary phase and dissolving in the mobile phase.
\[R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by component}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}\] It is always between \(0\) and \(1\).
Components that dissolve well in the mobile phase travel further; strongly adsorbed ones stay low.
Identify substances by comparing Rf values with standards under identical conditions. Baseline in pencil, above the solvent.
topics.explain: Explain why two dyes separate on a TLC plate.

qs.q: A spot moves \(3.0\ \mathrm{cm}\) while the solvent front moves \(12.0\ \mathrm{cm}\). Find \(R_f\).
A component with a high Rf is…
o: strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase
more attracted to the mobile phase

qs.q: Why is the baseline drawn in pencil?
o: Ink would dissolve and run with the solvent

aos.name: Unit 1 AoS 2 · How are materials quantified and classified?

topics.title: The mole and formulas
points: One mole \(= 6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles (Avogadro’s constant, \(N_A\)).
Molar mass \(M\) (\(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) equals the relative mass from the periodic table.
\(n = \dfrac{m}{M}\) and \(n = \dfrac{N}{N_A}\)
\[\%\ \text{by mass} = \frac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol}}{M} \times 100\]
Empirical formula: grams in 100 g → divide by M → divide by the smallest → whole-number ratio.
Molecular formula \(=\) empirical formula \(\times \dfrac{M(\text{compound})}{M(\text{empirical formula})}\)
topics.explain: Explain the difference between an empirical and a molecular formula using glucose.

qs.q: How many moles are in \(10.0\ \mathrm{g}\) of NaOH (\(M = 40.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\))?
How many molecules are in 0.50 mol of water?
A hydrocarbon is 85.7% C and 14.3% H. Find its empirical formula.
What is the percentage by mass of hydrogen in water?
A compound has empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) and \(M = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\). What is its molecular formula?

topics.title: Organic compounds
points: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (-ane), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (-ene, C=C), alkynes (-yne, C≡C), haloalkanes (chloro- etc.), alkanols (-ol, –OH), carboxylic acids (-oic acid, –COOH).
Prefixes: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non, dec.
Name from the longest chain; number from the end nearest the functional group; branches as prefixes (2-methylpropane, but-2-ene, propan-1-ol).
Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different structure.
Longer chains: higher boiling point and viscosity, lower volatility. –OH and –COOH hydrogen-bond, so they boil higher.
Alkenes undergo addition across C=C; alkanes undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.
topics.explain: Explain why ethanol boils much higher than propane even though their molar masses are similar.

qs.q: What is the name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
qs.e: Longest chain is 4 C with a methyl on carbon 2.

qs.q: Which general formula belongs to alkenes?
What type of reaction occurs when ethene reacts with bromine?
qs.a: Addition: Br₂ adds across the double bond to form 1,2-dibromoethane.

qs.q: Butane and 2-methylpropane are…

topics.title: Polymers and plastics
points: Addition polymers form from monomers with C=C (ethene → polyethene). No by-product.
Condensation polymers form from monomers with a functional group at each end, releasing a small molecule (usually water): polyesters, nylon, proteins.
LDPE: many branches, low density, soft. HDPE: few branches, chains pack closely, denser and more rigid.
Thermoplastics have no cross-links and soften on heating (recyclable). Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links and char instead of melting.
Isotactic polymers (side groups all on one side) pack best and have the highest melting points.
Sustainability: mechanical and chemical recycling, bioplastics, biodegradable plastics, circular economy.
topics.explain: Explain why a thermoplastic can be recycled by melting but a thermoset cannot.

qs.q: Which monomer can form an addition polymer?
qs.e: It needs a C=C double bond.

qs.q: HDPE is more rigid than LDPE because…
o: its chains pack more closely, giving stronger dispersion forces

qs.q: What small molecule is usually released in condensation polymerisation?
A polymer that chars instead of melting when heated is…

aos.name: Unit 2 AoS 1 · How do chemicals interact with water?

topics.title: Properties of water
points: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules explains its unusual properties.
High specific heat capacity (\(4.18\ \mathrm{J\ g^{-1}\,{}^\circ C^{-1}}\)): oceans steady the climate. \(q = mc\Delta T\)
High latent heat of vaporisation (\(40.7\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and fusion (\(6.0\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)). \(q = nL\)
Ice is less dense than water because hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open hexagonal lattice.
Cohesion gives surface tension; adhesion gives capillary action and wetting.
topics.explain: Explain why lakes freeze from the top down and why that matters for fish.

qs.q: How much energy heats \(250\ \mathrm{g}\) of water from \(20\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(80\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\)?
How much energy boils \(36.0\ \mathrm{g}\) of water at \(100\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\)?
Why does ice float?
o: Air bubbles are trapped in it
Hydrogen bonds hold molecules further apart in a hexagonal lattice
It has a lower molar mass

qs.q: On a heating curve, the flat sections show…
qs.e: Energy goes into breaking hydrogen bonds, not raising temperature.

topics.title: Acids, bases and pH
points: Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate H⁺, bases accept H⁺. Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺.
Amphiprotic species can do both: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻.
Strong acids ionise completely (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄); weak acids partly (CH₃COOH). Strength is not concentration.
Acid + metal → salt + H₂. Acid + hydroxide or oxide → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.
\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). \(K_w = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.00 \times 10^{-14}\) at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
Each pH unit is a \(10\times\) change in \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). Diluting a strong acid \(10\times\) raises pH by \(1\).
topics.explain: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.

qs.q: What is the pH of \(0.010\ \mathrm{M}\) HCl?
Find the pH of \(0.010\ \mathrm{M}\) NaOH at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
What is the conjugate base of HSO₄⁻?
Write the products of hydrochloric acid reacting with calcium carbonate.
qs.a: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide: 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

qs.q: Which is amphiprotic?
qs.e: It can donate (→ CO₃²⁻) or accept (→ H₂CO₃) a proton.

topics.title: Redox and galvanic cells
points: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain. Oxidising agents are reduced.
Oxidation numbers: elements 0, simple ions = charge, O usually −2, H usually +1, total = charge.
Balance half equations in acid: atoms, then O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻.
More reactive metals displace less reactive metal ions: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
Galvanic cell: anode = oxidation (−), cathode = reduction (+). Electrons flow anode → cathode through the wire.
The salt bridge moves ions (anions to the anode, cations to the cathode), never electrons.
topics.explain: Explain what the salt bridge does and what would happen without it.

qs.q: What is the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
In a Zn | Cu galvanic cell, the anode is…
Balance: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ (acidic solution).
What does the salt bridge carry?

aos.name: Unit 2 AoS 2 · How are chemicals measured and analysed?

topics.title: Solubility and concentration
points: Solubility is the maximum mass dissolving in 100 g of water at a given temperature. Below the curve: unsaturated; on: saturated; above: supersaturated.
Most ionic solids are more soluble when hot; gases are less soluble when hot.
\(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) (\(V\) in litres). Other units: \(\mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}\), ppm (\(\mathrm{mg\ L^{-1}}\)), % (m/v).
Dilution: \(c_1V_1 = c_2V_2\)
1.0 M MgCl₂ contains 1.0 M Mg²⁺ and 2.0 M Cl⁻.
topics.explain: Explain why a fizzy drink goes flat faster when warm.

qs.q: \(50.0\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{M}\) HCl is diluted to \(500.0\ \mathrm{mL}\). Find the new concentration.
What is [Cl⁻] in 0.30 M CaCl₂?
How many moles of NaCl are in \(250\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(0.40\ \mathrm{M}\) solution?

topics.title: Titrations and stoichiometry
points: Stoichiometry: balanced equation → moles of known → mole ratio → convert to what is asked.
Limiting reagent: work out which reactant runs out first; it decides the amount of product.
Aliquot = pipette volume. Titre = burette volume. Concordant titres are within 0.10 mL.
Primary standard: pure, known formula, stable, does not absorb water.
Rinse burette and pipette with their own solution; rinse flasks with deionised water.
Burette rinsed with water → titre too large. Pipette rinsed with water → too few moles in aliquot.
topics.explain: Explain why rinsing the conical flask with water does not affect the result.

qs.q: \(20.00\ \mathrm{mL}\) of HCl needs \(18.50\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(0.100\ \mathrm{M}\) NaOH. Find \(c(\mathrm{HCl})\).
What volume of H₂ forms at SLC from 2.43 g Mg? (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂)
If the burette is last rinsed with water, the calculated concentration of the flask solution will be…
qs.e: The titrant is diluted, so a larger titre is needed.

qs.q: 4.0 g CH₄ reacts with 10.0 g O₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O). Which is limiting?
qs.e: 0.25 mol CH₄ needs 0.50 mol O₂ but only 0.3125 mol is present.

topics.title: Gases
points: Kinetic theory: gas particles move randomly, are far apart, have no forces between them and collide with the walls (pressure).
\(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101.3\ \mathrm{kPa} = 760\ \mathrm{mmHg}\). \(T(\mathrm{K}) = T(^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 273\)
Boyle \(p_1V_1 = p_2V_2\); Charles \(\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}\); combined \(\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}\) (kelvin only).
\(pV = nRT\) with \(p\) in kPa, \(V\) in L, \(R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\).
\(n = \dfrac{V}{V_m}\), where \(V_m = 24.8\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\) at SLC (\(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\)).
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.
topics.explain: Use kinetic theory to explain why heating a sealed can raises the pressure.

qs.q: A gas is \(3.00\ \mathrm{L}\) at \(27\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\). Find its volume at \(127\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(200\ \mathrm{kPa}\).
What volume does 0.200 mol of gas occupy at SLC?
At constant temperature, halving the volume of a gas will…
Use \(pV = nRT\) to find \(V\) for \(0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\) at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\).

topics.title: Analysis of salts
points: Sources of salts in water: minerals from rocks, heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd) from industry, organometallics such as methylmercury.
Gravimetric analysis: dissolve, precipitate with excess reagent, filter, wash, dry to constant mass, weigh, calculate.
A precipitate that is not fully dried makes the result too high.
Colorimetry and UV-visible spectroscopy: absorbance is proportional to concentration. Use standards to draw a calibration curve.
Choose a wavelength (or complementary-colour filter) where the substance absorbs most.
topics.explain: Explain why a precipitate must be dried to constant mass.

qs.q: \(0.466\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) (\(M = 233.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is collected. Find the mass of sulfate ions.
In UV-visible spectroscopy, the unknown’s concentration is found from…
A precipitate is weighed while still damp. The calculated amount will be…
